narrative:
The model's prediction indicates a 67.8% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. This means that, based on your academic profile, the odds are roughly two to one against you passing, which is the primary reason your law school application was denied. The admissions decision rests on this fundamental risk, as the school must protect its bar pass rates and your own investment in legal education.

Three factors mattered most in reaching this conclusion. Your LSAT score had the greatest influence on the decision, and it strongly pushed the prediction toward failure. At 23.50, your score is substantially below the average of 37.18 among accepted students, which signals significant concern about your readiness for the rigorous academic demands of law school and the bar exam itself. The second most influential factor was your class standing in your third year of undergraduate study. Being in the second decile places you well below the average of 5.79 among accepted students, indicating that your academic performance in your upper-level courses was considerably weaker than that of your peers who were admitted. This factor also pushed strongly in the direction of bar exam failure, suggesting a pattern of academic struggle that could carry into legal studies.

Your undergraduate GPA, however, actually pushed the prediction slightly toward passing. At 3.10, it is close to the accepted student average of 3.23, and this factor provided a modest counterbalance. Unfortunately, the combined influence of your LSAT score and third-year class standing far outweighed this positive signal.

To improve your chances, focus on retaking the LSAT after dedicated preparation and strengthen your academic record through additional coursework that demonstrates your ability to succeed in rigorous, exam-based environments.
